 Home Blog Still Scrambling To Meet The Tax Deadline? Four Ways To Make Next Year Easier Still Scrambling To Meet The Tax Deadline? Four Ways To Make Next Year Easier
 Guest Writer November 2, 2026 Blog With the end-of-October tax lodgement deadline fast approaching, many Australian small businesses may be facing a familiar scramble. Missing documents, delayed approvals, scattered records and endless email chains can quickly consume valuable time that business owners would rather spend serving customers and growing their business.
 While the immediate priority is meeting the deadline, the pressure of tax season can also expose the hidden inefficiencies in how a business operates. And with those frustrations fresh in mind, now is an opportunity to consider what could be done differently next year.
 Despite widespread discussion around digital transformation, many SMEs are still relying on manual processes. December 2025 MYOB research found just half of Australian SMEs use cloud-based digital tools for major workflows, suggesting many businesses have opportunities to reduce administrative burden by digitising key processes.
 While many conversations about enterprise technology adoption focus on the latest innovations, the biggest opportunity for SMEs is often much simpler: using the right tools to reduce administrative burden, improve visibility and make everyday workflows easier.
 Here are four practical ways businesses can learn from this year’s tax season and set themselves up for a more efficient year ahead.
 Start with your biggest admin bottleneck
 It can be tempting to adopt a new tool as soon as a process becomes frustrating. But investing in technology before identifying the underlying problem can add more systems, notifications and complexity without making work easier.
 With the challenges of tax season still fresh, start by looking at where the process slowed down most. Was it finding documents? Collecting approvals? Following up with clients or suppliers? Reconciling information across multiple systems? Ask the people involved in the process, too: they may have practical insights into the delays and repeated tasks that aren’t obvious from the outside.
 Once the bottleneck is clear, consider what would improve it. That might mean changing a process, making better use of software the business already has, or introducing a new tool. Defining the problem first makes it easier to assess whether a solution is working, for example, by tracking time saved, fewer follow-ups or fewer missing records.
 Technology should solve a problem, not create another one.
 Create a single source of truth for financial records
 Searching through emails, desktops, shared drives and multiple applications for tax documents is a common source of frustration. It can also make it harder for staff, accountants and external advisers to know whether they have the latest version or whether anything is missing.
 A central, secure location for financial records can reduce time spent searching and make collaboration simpler. The system doesn’t need to be complicated, but it should be consistent and clear. A shared folder structure, standardised file naming conventions, tax and compliance checklists, and appropriate access permissions can all help.
 It’s also worth agreeing on how documents should be saved and who is responsible for adding or checking them. Rather than waiting until the next tax deadline to gather important records, businesses can make document management part of their regular workflow.
 A well-organised document system helps everyone understand where records live, what’s complete and what still requires attention. That clarity is useful not just at tax time, but whenever the business needs to find information quickly.
 Less time searching means more time acting.
 Replace manual approvals with digital workflows
 Tax season often involves gathering signatures, approvals and confirmations from multiple stakeholders. Paper-based processes and lengthy email chains can create delays, make it difficult to see what’s outstanding and increase the risk of missed deadlines.

 Digital signature and approval platforms can help keep requests moving by making it easier to send documents, monitor progress and follow up when needed. Solutions such as Dropbox Sign enable businesses to send documents for signature, use reusable templates for recurring agreements, track completion status, automate reminders and maintain a clear audit trail.
 For example, an accounting practice collecting signed engagement letters from clients ahead of tax season could use digital signatures to reduce manual follow-ups and keep track of outstanding requests, rather than relying on individual emails and paperwork.
 Before introducing a digital workflow, consider who needs to review or sign each document, what order approvals should follow and how the completed record will be stored. It’s also important to check whether electronic signatures are appropriate for the relevant documents and requirements.
 A clear process, supported by the right tool, can make responsibilities and next steps more visible to everyone involved. Putting these workflows in place ahead of the next busy period can help create a more predictable and transparent approval process.
 Treat tax season as a workflow health check
 Busy periods can reveal where productivity is being lost. Australian Industry Group research found that improving productivity is the primary driver of technology investment among Australian businesses. Tax time can be a useful opportunity to spot the bottlenecks that are holding work back and consider whether they can be addressed.
 Look for recurring challenges, such as repeated requests for the same documents, frequent switching between applications, approval delays and manual data entry. These may point to unclear responsibilities, disconnected systems or steps that could be simplified or automated.
 The key is to turn those observations into lasting improvements rather than waiting until the next tax deadline approaches. That might mean introducing a regular document review, standardising recurring processes or agreeing on clearer responsibilities for managing information and approvals.
 Not every issue requires new technology. Some may be resolved by clarifying ownership, standardising a checklist or agreeing on a consistent way to store information. Where technology could help, these observations provide a more informed starting point for evaluating options.
 The lessons learned during busy periods can drive lasting operational improvements.
 Tax season is often viewed as a compliance exercise, but it can also be a valuable opportunity to assess how efficiently a business operates. The businesses that approach tax season with less stress won’t necessarily be those with larger teams or bigger budgets, but those that have taken steps to establish clearer processes and better visibility across their operations.
 By making a few practical improvements to how documents are stored, shared and signed, small businesses can build simpler, more efficient workflows that save time throughout the year.
